text: UNESCO inscribed the shared culture of çay in Türkiye and Azerbaijan on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2022. UNESCO describes tea as a social practice associated with hospitality, maintaining relationships, and marking important occasions. Communities primarily harvest and drink black tea; it is served freshly brewed and hot, commonly in small pear-shaped cups with sweets, sugar, lemon, jam, or dried fruit.
document__title: Culture of Çay (tea), UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

text: UNESCO inscribed the shared culture of çay in Azerbaijan and Türkiye on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2022. UNESCO describes tea as an important social practice for hospitality, social ties, and significant life events. Communities primarily harvest and drink black tea, served hot and freshly brewed in pear-shaped cups. In some Azerbaijani regions, local spices or herbs such as cinnamon, ginger, and thyme may be added; practices vary by community.
document__title: Culture of Çay (tea), UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

text: Saudipedia describes coffee followed by tea as part of Saudi hospitality etiquette, with tea sometimes served later when lunch or dinner is part of the occasion. Mint, speedwell, or other aromatic leaves may be added. Its description of ember tea says water and sugar are boiled in a jug over embers before coarse tea is added; this style is associated with outdoor camping. These are documented customs, not universal rules for every household.
document__title: Drinks in Saudi Arabia, Saudipedia

text: Jordan News Agency Petra reported the Jordanian Ministry of Culture heritage director describing tea as part of daily social and cultural life, including family visits and gatherings. The article notes that tea is often prepared with aromatic plants; examples mentioned by local researchers include mint, anise, and sage. It describes variation among urban, rural, and Bedouin communities, so these flavors should be treated as common examples rather than a single national recipe.
document__title: Tea's place in Jordanian popular memory and culture, Petra News Agency

text: Go Türkiye describes black tea as an everyday drink in Türkiye and a sign of friendship, hospitality, and courtesy. A common preparation uses a stacked çaydanlık: tea leaves steep in concentrated hot water in the upper pot, then the brew is diluted with hot water from the lower kettle to taste. Tea-growing provinces include Rize, Trabzon, Artvin, Ordu, and Giresun, with Rize especially prominent.
document__title: Tea as a Symbol of Common Life and Culture in Anatolia, Go Türkiye

text: An Iranian food-science study examines Gilan (Guilan) black tea and describes its processing steps as withering, rolling, fermentation (oxidation), and drying. The study compares brewing methods and measures chemical properties in laboratory conditions; it does not establish health benefits for consumers. Gilan is a tea-producing province in northern Iran on the Caspian Sea.
document__title: Processing and brewing of Gilan black tea, Journal of Food Science and Technology

text: ISO 20715:2023 classifies six basic tea types made from Camellia sinensis by their manufacturing processes: black, green, white, oolong, yellow, and dark tea. Herbal or fruit infusions that do not use Camellia sinensis are not one of these six tea types. A tea name based on flavor, shape, origin, or serving style may describe another dimension rather than a separate basic processing type.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Black tea processing under ISO 20715 includes withering, rolling or maceration, aeration/oxidation, and drying. The word fermentation is often used in tea trade for this enzyme-driven oxidation step; it does not necessarily mean microbes fermenting the leaves. This distinction helps explain why black tea is described as oxidized tea.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Green tea is made by quickly applying heat to fresh leaves to inactivate enzymes, followed by steps that may include rolling, shaping, or comminution, and drying. Compared with black tea, the defining processing contrast is that green tea is not intentionally aerated/oxidized through the black-tea process. Specific heating methods and shapes vary by region and product.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: White tea is described by ISO 20715 as harvested tea shoots that undergo one withering and drying stage. The term white tea therefore refers to a Camellia sinensis tea type and a processing approach, not to an infusion made from white-colored flowers or herbs.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Oolong tea is a partially oxidized tea type. ISO 20715 describes steps including withering, tumbling, partial aeration/oxidation, enzyme inactivation, rolling or shaping, and drying. Oolong is not a single oxidation percentage or flavor: production choices differ among origins and styles.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Yellow tea processing includes enzyme inactivation, rolling or shaping, a yellowing stage, and drying. The yellowing step is a distinguishing part of the process described in ISO 20715. Yellow tea is one of the six basic Camellia sinensis tea types in the standard.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Dark tea processing in ISO 20715 includes enzyme inactivation, rolling, piling fermentation, and drying. The piling stage distinguishes this post-fermented tea process from the enzyme-driven oxidation commonly called fermentation during black tea manufacture. Dark tea products and local methods vary; do not treat all dark teas as one recipe.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Matcha is produced from shade-grown tender tea leaves. ISO 20715 describes steaming to inactivate enzymes, drying the leaves without rolling, and fine grinding. Matcha is therefore a finely milled tea leaf product, not simply any powdered green tea; production methods and labeling should be checked for the product in question.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Scented tea, compressed tea, and instant tea can be further processed products made from basic tea types. Their format or added aroma does not necessarily create a seventh basic tea type. For example, a scented tea may be based on green or black tea, while a compressed tea describes its shape.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Herbal tea, tisane, and fruit infusion are common beverage labels but may not be tea made from Camellia sinensis. ISO's six basic tea types all refer to tea produced from Camellia sinensis. If a customer asks about caffeine or tea origin, first determine whether the product contains tea leaves or only herbs, spices, flowers, or fruit.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: A flavored tea and a scented tea are product descriptions rather than separate basic tea types. Flavoring can be added to a tea base, while scenting may transfer aroma from aromatic materials during processing. To identify the underlying tea, check whether the base is black, green, oolong, white, yellow, or dark tea and whether ingredients or aroma sources are listed.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Tea type suggests a starting point for brewing, but it does not prescribe one universal time or temperature. Leaf grade, particle size, cultivar, water, quantity, and desired strength all affect extraction. Fine CTC particles generally infuse faster than larger whole leaves, so follow the producer's directions and adjust to taste rather than assuming one brewing formula applies to every tea.
document__title: ISO 20715:2023 Tea — Classification of tea types

text: Tea taxonomies can vary by country, tradition, and the purpose of classification. A useful general reference is the ISO process-based classification, but local market terms may group products by oxidation, processing method, appearance, or customary name. When answering what kind of tea a product is, distinguish the leaf processing category from its origin, cultivar, grade, flavoring, and retail form.
document__title: Typology of Processed Tea

text: In Chinese-language tea categories, hongcha is commonly called black tea in English, even though brewed hongcha liquor often appears reddish. This is a translation convention, not a claim that hongcha is the same product as Chinese heicha, which is usually translated as dark tea. Ask about the processing tradition or origin if a user says only black tea, because English naming can be ambiguous across markets.
document__title: Typology of Processed Tea

text: A practical tea product description can combine several attributes: basic processing type, cultivar, origin, manufacturing style, grade, added ingredients, and product form. For example, a product can be described as black tea from a named origin, made by orthodox processing, scented with jasmine, and sold loose leaf. These attributes answer different questions and should not be collapsed into a single tea-family label.
document__title: Typology of Processed Tea

text: Tea cultivar and tea type are different concepts. Cultivar describes the cultivated plant selection; black, green, oolong, white, yellow, and dark tea describe processed product types. A research study indexed by FAO AGRIS reports that processing one cultivar by six typical methods produced differentiated chemical profiles. Therefore, cultivar alone does not determine the finished tea type or its aroma; processing also matters.
document__title: Impact of Six Typical Processing Methods on the Chemical Composition of Tea Leaves

text: Orthodox and CTC refer to manufacturing approaches, not to the same classification axis as the six basic tea types. Tea Board India describes Orthodox tea as tea manufactured according to accepted orthodox processing norms and recognizes orthodox production for black and green tea. CTC means crush, tear, curl and describes a method that produces small, even particles; it is commonly used for strong infusions and tea bags. Product labels and regional standards should be checked because terms can be used differently in markets.
document__title: Tea Board India — Modalities and Scheme Guidelines

text: Darjeeling, Assam, and Nilgiri are origin-associated tea terms, while Orthodox describes a manufacturing style. Tea Board India guidelines tie protected or registered regional designations to production in the relevant area and registration requirements. Thus an origin name is not interchangeable with a processing category, and a tea made in an orthodox style is not automatically Darjeeling, Assam, or Nilgiri tea.
document__title: Tea Board India — Modalities and Scheme Guidelines

text: In black tea manufacture, the industry word fermentation commonly refers to enzymatic oxidation after leaf disruption and exposure to air. It is distinct from microbial fermentation. Green tea is made with little or no intentional oxidation, while oolong is partially oxidized. Dark tea may involve a separate piling or post-fermentation stage. When users ask whether tea is fermented, clarify which process they mean.
document__title: Fermentation: The Key Step in Processing of Black Tea
